newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algeria coalition seen leaving real power unchanged.
newsitem.headline: Algeria coalition seen leaving real power unchanged.

text.p: Algeria's leaders have set up a coalition government with the president's men keeping their grip on main ministries but giving moderate Islamists and old guard politicians a taste of more power in problem portfolios.
"It's government continuity in the important posts -- finance, foreign, interior, justice," said a Western diplomat on Thursday.
"There's no gigantic shift in policy. But they've given the junior partners, Hamas, or the MPS, and the National Liberation Front (FLN), the 'sticky' ministries. "
The MPS (Movement of a Peaceful Society), a moderate Islamist party, was formerly known as Hamas but changed its name to meet election laws barring the use of Islam as a party platform.
It came second in the June 5 general election, winning 69 seats against the 156 of the National Democratic Rally (RND) of backers of President Liamine Zeroual. The FLN took 62.
Zeroual reappointed Prime Minister Ahmed Ouyahia two weeks ago to form a government in which the RND has 62 percent of the posts.
"It took a long time to get everyone in place, longer than we thought it would, suggesting difficulties," said another diplomat.

Le Matin newspaper said Wednesday's announcement unveiled a "compromise of high risk", paralleling analysts' earlier comments that Algeria's 29 million people wanted real change while such a coalition would not reflect this.
Algeria has been battered by nearly six years of violence in which about 60,000 people have died since the authorities in 1992 cancelled a general election dominated by radical Islamists.
The radicals have been outlawed, chased out of town halls they won in 1990, and local elections are due this year to consolidate the political map envisaged by Zeroual.
Commentator Ahmed Outoudert said the line-up was not really a coalition but one in which Ouyahia had manoeuvred to share out difficult ministries and keep his hands on the purse strings.

"Ouyahia seems determined to maintain the course he has traced since his first nomination in January 1996, that is, to set in place the programme of the president...," Outoudert said, writing in Liberte newspaper on Thursday.
Zeroual has pursued a stringent policy of economic reform under a deal with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) which ends next April.

The centralised state economy is being opened up, austerity is de rigeur, and the government is pursuing a cautious privatisation policy, balancing the need to keep jobs where possible after years of bloated state industry.
Ouyahia has seen hard currency reserves reach $5 billion, inflation cut and the danger of a third rescheduling of Algeria's estimated $32 billion debt averted.
But the macroeconomic reform has brought hardship to many ordinary Algerians and added anxiety about job security to the security fears created by more than five years of violence.
The reform focus has also prevented any mass injection of cash into the economy to promote a major building programme to help resolve the desperate housing shortage and high unemployment.

The MPS and the FLN, which ran Algeria for three decades of socialist rule, each have four ministerial portfolios out of the 28. The MPS used to have two portfolios. Both parties also each have three posts of secretary of state.
MPS posts include industry and small and medium enterprises.

"Both those are difficult. Industrial output has been falling and it will not be easy to reverse. But the party has for years been arguing for faster economic change so perhaps it is well suited for this," said a European diplomat.
The FLN also has a key and difficult portfolio, agriculture, with much of Algeria, already one of the world's biggest hard wheat importers, having been hit by drought this year.
Despite the lack of change and there being no real voice for Moslem fundamentalists in the government, one diplomat said he did not believe Algerians would necessarily be disappointed.
"In the end, what is going to make people for or against the government will be if it tackles key areas like the housing and jobs shortage, water problems...," he said.
"Most people are more concerned about getting water into their taps, which comes now once every three days, than in ideological change."

Algeria is short of about two million homes, according to officials, and has more than two million people out of work in a workforce of around six million. Officials have said it was these factors, breeding lack of hope, that fuelled Islamist ranks.
"That's the real challenge -- can they find a base consensus among these three parties to give people hope?" the diplomat said.
